analysis.investment_thesis: EIH is a high-quality luxury hotel stalwart (Oberoi brand) with pristine balance sheet and exceptional margins, but at P/E 26.5x with revenue growing only ~9% and earnings growth decelerating to ~14%, the PEG sits near 1.9 — well above my comfort zone of 1.0. This is a quality business priced for quality, not a ten-bagger.
key_strengths: Near-zero debt (D/E 0.05) with net cash position (Cash 378 Cr vs Debt 265 Cr) — fortress balance sheet in a capital-heavy sector
Exceptional operating margins of 38.91% — among the best in Indian hospitality, reflecting true luxury pricing power of the Oberoi brand
ROCE of 23.4% and improving OCF (825 Cr in FY25) confirm the asset base is genuinely productive post-COVID recovery
key_risks: Revenue CAGR is only 5.7% over 9 years and only 9.2% in FY25 — too slow for a P/E of 26.5x; PEG ≈1.9 based on trailing earnings growth fails my <1.0 test
Capex surging to 485 Cr in FY25 (3.5x FY23 levels), CWIP at 403 Cr — free cash flow compressed to 346 Cr from 494 Cr despite higher EBITDA; execution risk on expansion

Hotels are quintessential cyclicals; the 9Y income statement shows devastating COVID impact (net loss 375 Cr in FY21) — the recent P/E expansion prices in a smooth runway that history doesn't guarantee
red_flags: Forward P/E (26.82) nearly identical to trailing P/E (26.50) — the market is pricing in essentially zero near-term earnings growth, making the current multiple hard to justify
Net profit 9Y CAGR of 20.6% is flattering — it is anchored to a 143 Cr base in FY16 and a massive COVID trough; normalized forward growth is likely 12-15%, pushing PEG above 1.8
analysis.detailed_analysis:
EIH is a stalwart-cyclical in Lynch's taxonomy — an iconic brand (Oberoi) with wide moat characteristics but fundamentally tied to travel cycles. The business quality is undeniable: 38.9% operating margins, 23.4% ROCE, and a nearly debt-free balance sheet are attributes you rarely see in capital-intensive hospitality. OCF has recovered strongly to 825 Cr in FY25, and the company is clearly in reinvestment mode (capex jumped to 485 Cr, CWIP at 403 Cr) suggesting management is betting on India's luxury travel boom — a story I can see from the consumer side.

The problem is price. At P/E 26.5x with revenue compounding at just 5.7% over nine years and only 9.2% in FY25, the stock is priced like a fast grower but growing like a stalwart. My PEG check — using the realistic 13-15% forward earnings growth — delivers a PEG around 1.7-1.9, a clear red flag in my framework. The surging capex is also compressing FCF (346 Cr in FY25 vs. 494 Cr in FY24) right as the growth multiple demands proof of acceleration. I'd revisit at a P/E of 18-20x or if revenue growth consistently exceeds 15% for two consecutive years — until then, hold existing positions but don't add aggressively.
